routes.description: Establish a cumulative historical inference from bodily appearance testimony, the empty tomb, witness transformations, and comparative miracle evidence to Jesus's physical resurrection.
routes.successCriteria: The combined evidence must make a physical resurrection a historically reasonable explanation with greater explanatory unity than the proposed visionary, literary, relocation, or theft alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative historical evidence specifically to Jesus returning bodily from death.

centralBridges.description: Establish that the earliest appearance traditions concern an embodied Jesus and include individual and group encounters.
Establish a known burial followed by a genuinely missing body that natural alternatives do not explain as economically.
Connect sincere testimony, costly proclamation, and prominent conversions to experiences requiring a historical explanation.
Show that rival miracle traditions and visionary models do not match the relevant resurrection evidence closely enough to neutralize it.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Supply historically credible transmission through Paul, Luke, and restrained canonical narratives.
Keep supernatural causation available as a historical explanatory category rather than excluding it in advance.

routes.description: Show that the surviving testimony is too indirect, ambiguous, and comparable to rival religious claims to warrant a historical conclusion of physical resurrection.
routes.successCriteria: The evidence must remain compatible with visionary development, literary construction, ordinary movement dynamics, or natural tomb histories without requiring Jesus's bodily return from death.

motionBridge.description: Prevent the available historical record from warranting the specific conclusion that Jesus physically rose from death.

centralBridges.description: Establish the absence of secure firsthand corroboration for group encounters with a physically resurrected Jesus.
Show that early visionary ambiguity and later narrative elaboration can account for the appearance traditions.
Demonstrate that comparable miracle witnesses, persecution, and movement growth do not reliably discriminate supernatural truth.
Keep relocation, theft, uncertain burial, or literary construction available as explanations of the tomb traditions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require evidence that informed witnesses suffered specifically for firsthand belief in a bodily resurrection.
Identify independent corroboration as a missing support for the reported postmortem appearances.

sections.title: Appearance testimony and bodily resurrection
sections.rationale: The motion requires not merely survival or religious experience but a physical resurrection, making the content and historical basis of the reported appearances indispensable.

sections.title: Source access and visionary interpretation
sections.rationale: The inference depends on whether the surviving sources provide reliable access to public encounters or remain compatible with visionary experiences and later transmission.

sections.title: Rival miracle claims and comparative standards
sections.rationale: Comparisons with Mormon and other miracle traditions test whether the evidential standards applied to Christian testimony discriminate the resurrection claim without special pleading.

sections.title: Sincerity, conversion, and persecution
sections.rationale: Conversions and costly proclamation matter only insofar as they connect informed sincerity and witness access to the specific claim of bodily resurrection.

sections.title: Empty tomb and natural alternatives
sections.rationale: A missing body supplies a distinct route toward bodily resurrection, while burial uncertainty, relocation, theft, and narrative construction provide competing explanations.

chunk-001:c001.proposition: Group appearances reported by Paul and Luke provide historical grounds for concluding that Jesus was alive after his death.

chunk-001:c002.proposition: Well-attested Marian apparitions raise the probability of Jesus's resurrection because such events fit Christian theology better if the resurrection occurred.

chunk-001:c003.proposition: Christian apparition reports do little to establish resurrection because comparable experiences occur elsewhere and the sources are unclear about whether Jesus's risen body was physical.

chunk-001:c004.proposition: Mormon witness and transfiguration traditions are at least comparable to early Christian appearance testimony, exposing how little can be verified about Paul's five-hundred-person report.

chunk-001:c005.proposition: Paul taught embodied resurrection rather than disembodied survival, and the physical features of Jesus's appearances distinguish them from acknowledged visions.

chunk-001:c007.proposition: Mormon miracle and witness claims are materially weaker analogues because natural incentives, prior expectations, source discrepancies, and contrary historical evidence reduce their credibility.

chunk-001:c008.proposition: The alleged expectation and financial-interest differences between Mormon and Christian witnesses are unstable because Jesus predicted resurrection and Mary Magdalene supported his ministry.

chunk-001:c009.proposition: Persecution and movement growth do not distinguish early Christianity from Mormonism, while the historical basis for claiming that apostles accepted death for resurrection belief is sparse.

chunk-002:c002-02.proposition: Paul is unclear about a physical resurrection, while later Gospel appearance narratives become more elaborate and theological rather than supplying secure eyewitness history.

chunk-002:c002-07.proposition: Luke is historically reliable and close to Paul, while Paul's encounter was comparable to apostolic appearances and the bounded appearance tradition resists a hallucination hypothesis.

chunk-002:c002-08.proposition: Apostolic suffering matters as evidence of sincere testimony by people positioned to know, and Christianity has additional explanatory features absent from the Mormon parallel.

chunk-003:chunk-003-c01.proposition: The canonical tomb narratives display historically credible restraint, and their women witnesses and imperfect guard story are unlikely apologetic inventions.

chunk-003:chunk-003-c02.proposition: Women discovering the tomb is narratively expected rather than an embarrassment criterion, while their immediate recourse to men and conflicting sequences weaken the apologetic inference.

chunk-003:chunk-003-c05.proposition: Evidence for Jesus before crucifixion is substantially stronger than evidence for postmortem appearances because the latter lacks independent extra-Christian corroboration.

chunk-003:chunk-003-c06.proposition: The resurrection explains the conversions of prior unbelievers and persecutors and the transformation of frightened apostles into bold proclaimers.

chunk-003:chunk-003-c07.proposition: Persecution and martyrdom do not establish eyewitness knowledge of a bodily resurrection because the clearest early cases concern visionary experiences or unspecified beliefs.

chunk-003:chunk-003-c09.proposition: An empty tomb, if there was one, is plausibly explained by temporary emergency burial followed by relocation or theft, neither of which requires resurrection.

chunk-003:chunk-003-c10.proposition: Non-resurrection is only an umbrella for multiple specific hypotheses whose conjunction reduces probability, and grave robbery poorly fits the retained burial goods and known practices.

chunk-004:chunk004-candidate-06.proposition: Paul's reported experience was not purely private or mental because his traveling companions also perceived an external manifestation.

chunk-004:chunk004-candidate-07.proposition: Visionary appearances need not be false, but their possible truth does not by itself establish that Jesus appeared in a physically resurrected body.
